title: What Is Desktop Publishing (1985)? — Definition
body:
Printing is mass-producing text and images: Gutenberg's movable type, the iron hand press, steam-powered cylinder presses, Linotype's hot-metal line casting (1886), Monotype's single-type casting, offset lithography, and the phototypesetting that bridged hot metal to digital.

In the context of this database, the Desktop Publishing (1985) is presented as one printing record among the printing and publishing history family. 1985's trinity: Mac, LaserWriter, PageMaker — the composing room's end.

title: Origins and History of Desktop Publishing (1985)
body:
The Desktop Publishing (1985) belongs to the 1985–present era and traces to Apple/Adobe/Aldus.

Gutenberg's movable type (c. 1440) made books reproducible; the iron hand press (Stanhope, 1800) strengthened the pull. Koenig's steam cylinder press (1814) printed The Times at 1,100 sheets/hour; Hoe's rotary (1843) and web perfecting presses fed the penny press. Ottmar Mergenthaler's Linotype (1886) — 'the eighth wonder' — let one operator cast whole lines of type as slugs, revolutionizing newspapers. Tolbert Lanston's Monotype (1887) cast single sorts for fine book work. Offset lithography (1904) replaced letterpress for most work; phototypesetting (1940s–70s) replaced hot metal; desktop publishing (1985) replaced the composing room.

Within that longer story, Desktop Publishing (1985): The WYSIWYG; the font's desktop. The DTP is publishing's revolution.

title: How Desktop Publishing (1985) Works
body:
Letterpress prints from raised, inked type pressed into paper (kiss or deep impression). The Linotype operator types on a 90-key keyboard; matrices drop from the magazine, assemble in a line, and molten type metal (lead/tin/antimony) is injected to cast a slug — then matrices redistribute automatically. Monotype casts individual characters from perforated paper-tape input. Offset lithography uses the chemistry of grease vs water on a plate: ink sticks to image areas, water to non-image, offset via rubber blanket to paper.

Applied to the Desktop Publishing (1985) (1985–present, Apple/Adobe/Aldus): The DTP is publishing's revolution.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of Desktop Publishing (1985) — Components
body:
Every Desktop Publishing (1985) is an assembly of the printing and publishing history family's standard parts:

• Type / sorts — Individual metal characters in cases (upper/lower).
• Chase & furniture — Iron frame and wooden blocks locking type in the press.
• Platen / cylinder — Impression mechanisms pressing paper to type.
• Linotype magazine — 90-channel matrix storage; the machine's library.
• Matrix — Brass mold for one character; assembles into lines.
• Metal pot — Molten type metal at ~550 F; the hot heart.
• Stereotype plate — Curved duplicate plates for rotary presses.
• Litho plate — Aluminum plate with image/non-image chemistry.
• Blanket cylinder — Rubber offset between plate and paper.
• Ink & rollers — Distribution train milling ink to a thin film.

When examining a surviving Desktop Publishing (1985), identify these parts in order: Type / sorts, Chase & furniture, Platen / cylinder, Linotype magazine, Matrix, Metal pot.

title: Printing and Publishing History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of printing and publishing history:

• slug — Linotype-cast line of type; also the machine's nickname ('the eighth wonder').
• pi — Spilled type; 'mind your p's and q's' from sorting.
• hellbox — Bin for worn type; 'gone to hell' in pieces.
• furniture — Wood/metal spacing locking type in the chase.
• quoin — Expanding wedge locking the forme.
• make-ready — Packing the press for even impression.
• offset — Litho printing via rubber blanket; the 20th century's workhorse.
• halftone — Dot screens rendering photos in print.
• composing stick — Hand compositor's type holder.
• galley — Tray holding set type before page makeup.
• proof — Test pull for correction; 'galley proof'.
• blueprint / diazo — White-line copying for drawings and proofs.

title: Desktop Publishing (1985) in Culture
body:
'Mind your p's and q's', 'out of sorts', 'hellbox', 'uppercase/lowercase' — printers gave English its metaphors. The Linotype's clatter was the soundtrack of democracy's daily edition; hot-metal composing rooms smelled of ink, oil, and molten lead. Letterpress's deep impression is now luxury stationery's signature.

The Desktop Publishing (1985) carries that cultural charge directly: The DTP is publishing's revolution.

title: Desktop Publishing (1985) Restoration Guide
body:
Clean presses mechanically; oil per charts. Type metal: mind lead hygiene (gloves, ventilation, no food). Matrix magazines need cleaning for smooth drops. Rubber rollers recondition or replace; check blankets for packing.

Restoration order for a Desktop Publishing (1985): 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical printing record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: Desktop Publishing (1985) — Linotype line-justification caster (Runnable Python)
body:
Simulates Linotype justification: matrices assemble, spacebands expand to fill the measure, and the line casts — with em-quad math from the composing room.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Desktop Publishing (1985) so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Linotype justification simulator (public-domain composing math)
PICA_PT = 12

def cast_line(words, measure_picas, body_pt=10):
    measure_pts = measure_picas * PICA_PT
    # rough widths: avg char ~0.5 em
    em = body_pt
    text_pts = sum(len(w) * 0.5 * em for w in words)
    gaps = len(words) - 1
    if gaps <= 0:
        return " ".join(words)
    space_needed = measure_pts - text_pts
    # Linotype spacebands expand wedge-wise to justify
    per_gap = space_needed / gaps
    em_space = per_gap / em
    line = (" " * 1).join(words)
    return {"line": line, "measure": measure_picas, "gaps": gaps,
            "spaceband_expansion_em": round(em_space, 2),
            "justified": space_needed >= 0}

r = cast_line("THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS".split(), 24)
print(f"measure {r['measure']} picas, {r['gaps']} spacebands expand "
      f"{r['spaceband_expansion_em']} em each -> justified={r['justified']}")
print("slug cast: |" + r["line"] + "|")
